frameworks.name: Agentic RAG for Outlook
frameworks.definition: A high-level method to turn an email mailbox into a retrieval-augmented system that can plan, retrieve relevant messages, and execute limited actions safely.
steps: Define use-cases and scope (triage, drafting, follow-ups) and acceptable automation levels.
Ingest mail incrementally and maintain message metadata and thread identifiers.
Normalize and clean content (strip signatures/quoted history, dedupe, preserve thread context).
Index with hybrid retrieval (vector + keyword) and rich metadata for filtered queries.
Expose retrieval as a callable tool/function the agent can use during planning.
Design agent prompts and planner behaviour to decide when to search, draft, or act.
Implement action gating (approval, test-sandbox, rate limits) before permitting sends.
Monitor performance, audit actions, and iterate prompts/indexing based on failures.
frameworks.when_to_use: When you need the assistant to do more than answer queries — to prioritise, draft and execute email workflows across a large mailbox.
failure_modes: Hallucination: agent produces authoritative but unfounded replies.
Over-automation: incorrect or inappropriate outbound messages sent without review.
Context loss: fragmented threads leading to wrong decisions.
Privacy/compliance breaches from excessive indexing or metadata leaks.
Operational drift: index staleness or retrieval degradation over time.

frameworks.name: Action Governance for Email Agents
frameworks.definition: A control framework to permit agent-initiated email actions while limiting business, legal and reputational risk.
steps: Classify actions into read-only, suggested-draft, and direct-send categories.
Apply least-privilege: grant minimal scopes and segregate test/sandbox accounts.
Require human review for high-risk categories (legal, regulatory, executive).
Introduce soft-launch: log actions, run in suggestion-only mode, then gradual enablement.
Maintain immutable audit logs and easy rollback paths for agent actions.
Define measurable KPIs (accuracy of drafts, false-send rate, user override frequency).
frameworks.when_to_use: Before enabling any agent capability that drafts or sends emails on behalf of users or systems.
failure_modes: Insufficient monitoring: undetected incorrect outbound messages.
Permission creep: agents gain broader access than intended.
User mistrust: excessive false positives or irrelevant actions reduce adoption.

frameworks.name: Email Retrieval Design (Hybrid + Metadata)
frameworks.definition: A retrieval-first design to ensure precision and context by combining vector similarity with structured metadata filters.
steps: Define an index schema that includes sender, recipients, date, threadId, categories and other business tags.
Use hybrid search (semantic vectors + keyword/lexical filters) to handle synonyms and exact matches.
Preserve and reconstruct thread context at retrieval time to avoid isolated-snippet errors.
Apply recency and sender-based ranking heuristics for prioritisation in triage scenarios.
Surface provenance snippets and message identifiers so agents and users can validate answers.
frameworks.when_to_use: When you need accurate, auditable retrieval from long-running email archives where both semantic recall and exact matching matter.
failure_modes: Poor metadata quality leading to irrelevant filters.
Snippet-level answers that omit critical thread context.
Over-reliance on semantic results for regulatory or legal queries that need verbatim evidence.

playbooks.title: Convert Mailbox into a Searchable RAG Knowledge Base
playbooks.trigger: You need reliable retrieval and contextual answers from an executive or project mailbox.
steps: Clarify business goals, data retention and compliance boundaries with legal/IT.
Select scope: which mailboxes, date ranges and folders to include.
Design metadata schema (sender, recipients, receivedDate, threadId, tags) to support filtering.
Choose a hybrid retrieval approach (vector + keyword) and a managed or hosted vector store.
Wrap retrieval as a callable tool the agent can use; require provenance display.
Run a pilot: validate retrieval quality against a representative query set.
Operationalise: schedule incremental ingests, monitoring and periodic re-indexing.
playbooks.applicable_when: Useful for teams needing searchable institutional memory, client correspondence discovery, or rapid evidence retrieval from mail archives.

playbooks.title: Pilot and Rollout for Agentic Email Assistant
playbooks.trigger: Stakeholders want an assistant that triages, drafts, and optionally sends email for specific user groups.
steps: Start with a tightly-scoped pilot group and limited automation (suggestion-only mode).
Define acceptance criteria (draft accuracy, override rate, user satisfaction).
Implement send-capability as staged: sandbox → supervised send → limited direct-send.
Enforce human-in-the-loop for high-risk messages and keep immutable logs.
Collect metrics and user feedback; iterate prompt templates, retrieval heuristics and metadata.
Scale gradually by expanding user groups, use-cases, and automation thresholds.
playbooks.applicable_when: When introducing an agent to real users and you need low-risk, measurable adoption with governance controls.

claims.text: Agentic RAG combines retrieval, multi-step reasoning (planning), and action execution.
claims.source_excerpt: Agents combine retrieval + reasoning + action. They can plan ("find today’s unread customer escalations"), retrieve (vector search across mail), and then act (draft replies or file tickets)

claims.text: Hybrid search (vector similarity plus lexical / BM25 scoring) is recommended to handle both semantic recall and long-tail keyword queries.
claims.source_excerpt: Hybrid search: enable vector + BM25 scoring for long-tail keyword queries.

claims.text: Managed 'knowledge agent' offerings (e.g., in Azure AI Search) were introduced to support agentic retrieval workflows.
claims.source_excerpt: Microsoft’s own “Knowledge Agents” objects in Azure AI Search were introduced precisely for this purpose.

glossary.one_line: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: LLM responses grounded by retrieved documents to reduce hallucination.
An extension of RAG where the system plans, retrieves, and can execute actions (e.g., send email).
Large language model: a statistical model that generates text conditioned on input prompts and context.
A numeric vector that represents text semantics for similarity search and retrieval.
A datastore optimised for nearest-neighbour search over embeddings to retrieve semantically similar documents.
The amount of text an LLM can attend to at once; affects how much conversation or documents it can consider.
A reusable structured prompt with placeholders used to standardise LLM instructions and context.
A component that selects relevant documents from an index to provide grounding for generation.
When an LLM outputs plausible-sounding but factually incorrect or unsupported information.
Microsoft’s managed service for hybrid search offering vector and lexical search plus agentic features.
A toolkit that composes LLMs, retrievers and tools into chains and agent workflows (high-level orchestration).
A multi-agent orchestration framework for building complex, actor-model agent workflows and planners.
A platform for running and managing local or on-prem language models for privacy-conscious deployments.
A high-performance library for efficient nearest-neighbour search over vector embeddings (commonly referenced).
A vector database for storing and searching embeddings, often used as an alternative to managed vector stores.

frameworks.name: RAG 2.0 — pragmatic blueprint for scaling
frameworks.definition: A practical, production-minded RAG architecture pattern that separates ingestion, embedding, vector storage, retrieval, re-ranking and LLM/agent services to enable scale and observability.
steps: Ingestion worker writes raw messages and metadata to a durable store (Postgres or equivalent).
Separate embedding worker consumes new records and writes vectors plus metadata to a vector store.
Use a dedicated vector DB (disk-backed) for first-stage retrieval; store metadata for filtering.
Run a second-stage cross-encoder re-ranker on the top-k candidates to produce the final doc set.
Host LLM/agent service behind an API that consumes re-ranked docs and returns streaming responses.
Split responsibilities into distinct services/containers (ingest, embed, retriever+re-rank, llm/agent) for independent scaling.
Add monitoring, structured logs and latency metrics for each stage.
frameworks.when_to_use: When the RAG app must move beyond hobby/prototype scale (concurrent users, >100k messages, frequent rebuilds) while keeping deploy complexity manageable.
failure_modes: Over-engineering for small datasets — added complexity without benefit.
Metadata mismatch between DB and vector store causing incorrect filtering.
Re-ranker model too large or poorly tuned, adding latency that offsets retrieval gains.
Insufficient observability — hard to find which stage causes slowdowns.

frameworks.name: Incremental RAG Performance Upgrade (surgical changes)
frameworks.definition: A prioritized sequence of local, low-risk changes that materially reduce latency and cost without a full rewrite or cloud migration.
steps: Load vector index lazily and in a way that reduces RAM pressure at cold start.
Add an on-disk embedding cache so repeated texts reuse embeddings.
Introduce a lightweight cross-encoder re-ranker after first-stage retrieval to boost quality.
Run heavy inference/IO-bound stages in background threads or executors to avoid blocking UIs.
Remove duplicate or legacy ETL/pipeline code to avoid accidental double-builds.
Chunk long documents before embedding to improve recall and keep index compact.
Compress or quantize the built index to reduce disk and memory footprint.
Scope searches by metadata (e.g., channel) via post-filtering to cut effective working set.
frameworks.when_to_use: When you need measurable performance and cost improvements in days-to-weeks and want to keep existing infra (local FAISS/SQLite).
failure_modes: Cache invalidation errors leading to stale retrieval results.
Re-ranker increases per-query latency if model size or batching is not managed.
Index compression that reduces quality more than expected if not validated.
Removing legacy code without ensuring single-source ETL causes data loss or missed records.

playbooks.title: Sprint: High-impact RAG app improvements
playbooks.trigger: Visible latency/cost problems, frequent cold-starts, or plan to support more users quickly.
steps: Create a perf-upgrades branch and add a short TODO manifest to track work.
Implement lazy loading / lower-memory footprint for the vector index to reduce cold starts.
Add an on-disk embedding cache to avoid re-embedding identical texts.
Bolt on a small cross-encoder re-ranker to improve final retrieval quality.
Run heavy RAG calls in background threads or executors so UIs remain responsive.
Prune duplicate or legacy pipeline code so ingestion is single-source-of-truth.
Chunk long documents before embedding and validate recall improvements.
Compress the built index to shrink disk and memory usage; validate quality.
Add simple channel-scoped post-filtering to speed common queries.
Run end-to-end performance tests and add basic metrics/logging for each stage.
playbooks.applicable_when: You have an existing monolithic RAG app (local FAISS + SQLite/Ollama) and want fast, low-risk wins without rearchitecting.

playbooks.title: Quick RAG architecture health check
playbooks.trigger: Need a concise answer to 'is this architecture good enough?' before scaling or pitching a refactor.
steps: Verify separation of concerns: ingestion, embeddings, retrieval, generation and UI should be distinct.
Check durable store suitability: is single-file SQLite becoming an I/O bottleneck?
Confirm embeddings are cached/reused and not re-generated per identical query.
Look for a second-stage re-ranking step; absence often limits answer quality.
Assess concurrency: are inference and retrieval synchronous and blocking front-ends?
Review deployment topology: one monolith vs split services and the impact on autoscaling.
Check for observability: per-stage latency metrics, structured logs and error traces.
playbooks.applicable_when: Preliminary audits, architecture reviews, or prior to committing to a larger rework or procurement decision.

claims.text: Design works for a few thousand messages but is not optimal once you cross >100k messages, concurrent users, or frequent index rebuilds.
claims.source_excerpt: Bottom line: the design works for a few thousand messages and low traffic, but it is not optimal once you cross (a) > 100k messages, (b) concurrent users, or (c) frequent index rebuilds.

claims.text: A single-file SQLite becomes I/O-bound once the database grows above ~1 million messages.
claims.source_excerpt: Single-file SQLite becomes I/O-bound once the DB grows (> 1 M msgs).

claims.text: Memory-mapping the FAISS index can drop cold-start time from ~30s to ~2s and reduce RSS by roughly 40–70%.
claims.source_excerpt: Cold-start drops from 30 s → 2 s; RSS shrinks by 40–70 %.

claims.text: An on-disk embedding cache can cut embedding requests by over 80% in typical usage.
claims.source_excerpt: Cuts embedding requests by > 80 % in typical usage → cheaper & faster.

claims.text: Adding a lightweight cross-encoder re-ranker after FAISS top-k can improve retrieval F1 by roughly 10–15%.
claims.source_excerpt: +10-15 F1 retrieval accuracy → noticeably better answers with zero LLM cost.

claims.text: Applying product quantisation during index build can make the FAISS index about 4–6× smaller with negligible quality loss.
claims.source_excerpt: 4-6× smaller index, faster similarity search, negligible quality loss.

glossary.one_line: An architecture that retrieves relevant documents and conditions an LLM on them to produce answers.
A statistical model trained on large text corpora to generate or complete natural language.
A numeric vector representing semantic content of text, used for similarity search.
A purpose-built store for vectors supporting nearest-neighbour search and metadata filtering (e.g., Qdrant).
A widely used library for efficient similarity search over dense vectors, commonly used locally or on-prem.
A model that scores document-query pairs jointly to produce higher-quality ranking than independent embeddings.
Technique that maps index files into process address space to reduce full RAM loading and speed cold starts.
An LLM-driven orchestrator that can call tools, follow chains, or perform multi-step reasoning in pipelines.
Techniques to shrink context (summaries, self-query, chunk selection) so more relevant content fits model limits.
A local model runtime used to host and query models on-prem or on a single host.

frameworks.name: Marco de evaluación de viabilidad concesional (España)
frameworks.definition: Estructura paso a paso para determinar si una carretera es candidata viable a concesión/PPP, integrando legal, fiscal, técnico, comercial y de mercado.
steps: Verificación jurídica: comprobar permissibilidad legal (Directiva 2014/23/UE, LCSP y normativa sectorial) y límites de la Administración competente.
Diagnóstico institucional: identificar responsable promotor (Estado, CCAA, diputación), competencias y capacidad de supervisión.
Prueba SEC/contabilidad: evaluar si el esquema puede quedar fuera de balance público según criterios SEC-2010 (transferencia real de riesgos).
Análisis de riesgos: mapear riesgos (construcción, disponibilidad, demanda, demanda mínima/garantías) y cuantificar exposición.
Modelo de ingresos y sensibilidad: construir proyecciones de tráfico/peajes o pagos de disponibilidad, con escenarios adversos y stress tests.
Estructura financiera: estimar necesidades de capital, apalancamiento posible sin garantías excesivas y apetito del mercado financiero.
Cláusulas contractuales clave: diseñar revisión de tarifas, mecanismos de equilibrio económico, limitaciones a garantías y condiciones de resolución.
Valor por dinero y fiscalidad: comparar alternativa pública tradicional (DBB) contra concesión en términos de VfM, coste total y riesgos fiscales.
frameworks.when_to_use: Evaluación estratégica y pre-factibilidad de proyectos viales en España para decidir ruta de contratación (concesión vs gestión pública).
failure_modes: Diseñar contratos con garantías implícitas que trasladan el riesgo al sector público (pérdida de off-balance).
Ignorar impacto de la Ley de Desindexación en revisión de tarifas y subestimar riesgo de costes crecientes.
Sobreestimación de demanda sin pruebas de mercado, provocando incumplimiento de ingresos y rescates.
Cláusulas de equilibrio mal calibradas que terminan neutralizando la transferencia de riesgo.
Falta de coordinación interinstitucional (promotor vs regulador) que bloquea ejecuciones o revisiones contractuales.

frameworks.name: Diagnóstico de transferencia de riesgo (concesiones conforme Directiva/TJUE)
frameworks.definition: Procedimiento para evaluar si un contrato realmente transfiere riesgos al privado, criterio decisivo para concesionalidad y tratamiento contable.
steps: Listar riesgos relevantes (construcción, demanda, disponibilidad, mantenimiento, operativos).
Identificar garantías y mecanismos públicos (aval, garantía de tráfico, ingresos mínimos, subvenciones recurrentes).
Cuantificar quién soporta la mayor parte de la pérdida en escenarios adversos (simulaciones soberanas).
Analizar cláusulas de restablecimiento del equilibrio y su efecto en la exposición privada al riesgo.
Revisar precedentes jurisprudenciales europeos y documentación que pruebe capacidad del privado para asumir riesgo.
Concluir: si el privado no está expuesto a incertidumbres relevantes, no habrá concesión genuina.
frameworks.when_to_use: Al diseñar o evaluar la estructura contractual de una concesión y para preparar la documentación justificativa ante auditorías contables o litigios.
failure_modes: Medir riesgos solo cualitativamente sin simular pérdidas cuantificadas.
Ignorar efectos de cláusulas de compensación automáticas que neutralizan pérdidas privadas.
Documentación insuficiente que impida justificar off-balance ante auditorías SEC o la Comisión Europea.

playbooks.title: Screening PPP para proyectos viarios (Checklist rápido)
playbooks.trigger: Promotor considera la opción de concesión/PPP para una carretera en fase pre-factibilidad.
steps: Confirmar competencia legal y normativa aplicable (Estado/CCAA; LCSP; Ley de Carreteras).
Aplicar filtro SEC-2010: identificar si existen garantías o compromisos públicos que puedan ligar deuda pública.
Realizar test de demanda: encargue un estudio de tráfico base y tres escenarios adversos/optimistas.
Diseñar alternativas contractuales (peaje directo, pago por disponibilidad, híbridos) y comparar riesgos.
Evaluar impacto de Ley 2/2015 (desindexación) en las fórmulas de revisión de precios propuestas.
Contactar con mercado financiero para sondear apetito y condiciones (sin ofrecer garantías que perjudiquen off-balance).
Decisión: avanzar a estudio de viabilidad financiera completo o reorientar a gestión pública.
playbooks.applicable_when: Primer filtro estratégico que debe aplicarse antes de gastar recursos en estudios de ingeniería o modelos financieros detallados.

playbooks.title: Playbook contractual: limitar riesgo de contabilización pública y ayudas de Estado
playbooks.trigger: Redacción de un pliego o negociación contractual para una concesión vial con financiación privada.
steps: Evitar cláusulas de garantía explícitas de ingresos o cobertura de deuda que superen el umbral de control público.
Limitar o condicionar garantías públicas (si imprescindibles) y documentar su excepcionalidad y temporalidad.
Diseñar mecanismos de equilibrio económico-financiero con triggers, prueba de causalidad y métodos de cálculo transparentes.
Establecer riesgo de demanda claramente asignado al concesionario cuando el modelo dependa de peajes.
Prever soluciones de renegociación que no automaticen compensaciones que anulen pérdidas privadas.
Documentar toda asignación de riesgos y análisis de sensibilidad para auditores SEC y verificadores de ayudas de Estado.
Incluir cláusulas de resolución y responsabilidad patrimonial de la Administración (RPA) con criterios objetivos.
playbooks.applicable_when: Durante la preparación de pliegos, negociación contractual o para validar ofertas del mercado financiero.

claims.text: La Directiva 2014/23/UE exige la transferencia efectiva del riesgo operacional al concesionario para que un contrato sea considerado concesión.
claims.source_excerpt: la Directiva 2014/23/UE ... exige la transferencia efectiva del riesgo operacional al concesionario como rasgo definitorio

claims.source_excerpt: la Ley 2/2015 de Desindexación ... prohíbe la indexación automática de contratos públicos a la inflación

claims.text: Las cláusulas de restablecimiento del equilibrio económico-financiero se usan para ajustar contratos ante cambios sustantivos, pero pueden erosionar la transferencia de riesgo.
claims.source_excerpt: Los contratos suelen incluir cláusulas de restablecimiento del equilibrio económico-financiero... Estas garantías contractuales deben diseñarse cuidadosamente para no vaciar de contenido el riesgo transferido.

claims.text: Si una concesión protege de facto al concesionario frente a pérdidas, la Comisión Europea puede considerarla una ayuda de Estado encubierta.
claims.source_excerpt: la Comisión Europea para evitar ayudas de Estado encubiertas en concesiones. Si un esquema concesional transfiere riesgos solo nominalmente pero garantiza de facto al concesionario beneficios ... podría considerarse una ayuda incompatible.

glossary.one_line: Norma UE que regula la adjudicación de contratos de concesión y exige transferencia efectiva de riesgo al concesionario.

glossary.term: LCSP (Ley de Contratos del Sector Público)
glossary.one_line: Ley española que transpone directivas UE sobre contratación pública, incluyendo concesiones en 2017.
Sistema Europeo de Cuentas; criterios que determinan si una PPP queda fuera del balance público.
Norma española que limita la indexación automática de contratos públicos a la inflación.
Criterio que exige que el concesionario asuma incertidumbres reales sobre construcción, operación o demanda.
Obligación de indemnizar al tercero por daños causados por la Administración en la gestión pública, aplicable en concesiones.
Cláusula que permite ajustar condiciones contractuales para mantener la viabilidad financiera ante cambios significativos.
Intervención pública que puede distorsionar la competencia; la UE vigila ayudas encubiertas en concesiones.
Modelo en que el usuario paga directamente por utilización (peaje) o mediante mecanismos de tarificación por uso.
Modelo PPP donde la administración paga por la disponibilidad del activo, transfiriendo distinto perfil de riesgo que el peaje.

frameworks.name: RAG App Repository Audit (non-destructive)
frameworks.definition: A structured, read-only audit method to map, trace, and prioritise issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation apps (Discord + Streamlit style).
steps: Stage 0: Create reporting folders (architecture/, reports/) and ensure dev tools available (or note absent).
Step 1 — Repo map: produce a tree of packages/files with one-line responsibility for each file.
Step 2 — Entry-point tracing: list depth‑1 and depth‑2 call graph for each main entry (Streamlit, bot, batch pipeline).
Step 3 — Tool & pipeline cross-check: verify tools metadata vs implementations; trace embedding/index read/write paths.
Step 4 — Static analysis sweep: run linters/tests, capture outputs into architecture/ for review.
Step 5 — Issue capture: record file:line, description, quick-fix, and assign severity.
Step 6 — Prioritise & package: sort by severity and produce REPO_MAP.md, INCONSISTENCIES.md and AUDIT_REPORT.md.
frameworks.when_to_use: Use before refactors or handoffs on RAG apps (where code evolved incrementally and may contain duplicate/legacy modules).
failure_modes: Running linters/tests without creating output directories leads to misleading zsh redirection errors.
Static-only audit misses runtime-only race conditions or API key issues (requires follow-up runtime checks).
Overwhelming the client with too many low‑severity findings; prioritisation step omitted.

frameworks.name: Agent-Tool Consistency Check (for LLM tool-calling workflows)
frameworks.definition: A focused checklist to ensure tools declared to an agent (metadata) exist, are importable, and are registered with the agent at runtime.
steps: Collect tool declarations from tools_metadata.py (or equivalent).
For each declared tool: locate implementing function in tools/ and confirm import path resolves statically.
Inspect agent bootstrap (core/agent.py) to confirm the tool is wired into the agent registry/dispatcher.
Flag mismatches: declared-but-missing, implemented-but-unregistered, or name/signature conflicts.
Produce a table: Tool | Declared? | Implemented? | Registered? | Suggested fix.
frameworks.when_to_use: When diagnosing unexpected agent behavior, silent failures in tool calls, or when merging legacy/duplicate tool modules.
failure_modes: Tools declared in metadata but with different names/signatures cause silent runtime failures.
Duplicate implementations across core/ and tools/ cause ambiguity about the canonical implementation.
Dynamic imports or string-based tool lookups increase false negatives in static checks.

frameworks.name: Embedding & Vector-Store Sanity Framework
frameworks.definition: A compact method to validate consistency across embedding creation, index persistence, and retrieval in vector-search pipelines.
steps: Identify all places that create embeddings and all places that read/write vector indexes (embed_store.py, rag_engine.py, data/).
Confirm single canonical index path or document divergent paths with a clear reconciliation plan.
Check for mismatched embedding dimensionality or model names referenced across modules.
Verify any ingest/update path calls update_index() (or equivalent) after new items are embedded.
Report non-atomic index operations (writes without locking/backups) and recommend safe update patterns.
frameworks.when_to_use: When search results degrade, indexes seem stale, or after migrating embedding models or index storage.
failure_modes: Multiple index directories become out-of-sync after partial pipeline runs.
Embedding dimension mismatch leads to silent runtime exceptions during similarity search.
Index writes performed without backup or versioning cause data loss on failed ingests.

playbooks.title: Cursor Copilot Audit Prompt — Single-Paste Execution
playbooks.trigger: You have a RAG + bot repo that evolved incrementally and you need a single-pass structural audit.
steps: Paste the prepared audit prompt into Cursor Copilot (include README or instruct Copilot to open it).
Ask Copilot to produce: REPO_MAP.md (module map), dependency graph, env_vars.md, and tools_inconsistencies.md.
Require static analysis logs saved under architecture/ (ruff, mypy, pytest) and insist on using mkdir -p architecture first.
Ask for a prioritized INCONSISTENCIES.md with file:line, severity, brief fix, and a short action plan.
Require Copilot to output progress messages like: 'Done – generated X' for each artefact.
playbooks.applicable_when: When engaging Cursor Copilot to run a comprehensive repository audit without performing code changes.

playbooks.title: Quick dev-tool and output-capture fix
playbooks.trigger: You see shell errors like 'zsh: no such file or directory: architecture/...' or 'command not found: ruff'.
steps: If redirection target missing: run mkdir -p architecture (or reports) before redirecting outputs.
If a tool binary is missing in venv: pip install --upgrade <tool> inside the activated venv (or add to requirements-dev.txt).
Prefer using tee to both view and persist long-running command outputs: ruff check . | tee architecture/ruff_output.txt.
Record the dev-tool versions you used into requirements-dev.txt for reproducibility.
playbooks.applicable_when: Local audit attempts fail due to missing directories or absent dev tools in the virtual environment.

playbooks.title: Non-destructive Static Analysis Sweep
playbooks.trigger: You want deterministic linter/test outputs saved for review and for a Copilot-assisted code audit.
steps: Create architecture/ and reports/ directories for artefacts.
Run linters and tests using pip-installed dev tools and capture outputs with tee.
Aggregate errors of severity E (or failing tests) into reports/static_analysis_summary.md.
Annotate the codebase with read-only TODO comments where fixes are straightforward and low-risk.
playbooks.applicable_when: Before refactoring or when onboarding external reviewers, to produce saved artefacts and baseline metrics.

claims.text: Create the output directory first (mkdir -p architecture) before redirecting command output to avoid 'no such file or directory' errors.
claims.source_excerpt:
zsh: no such file or directory: architecture/ruff_output.txt

`zsh: no such file or directory: architecture/…` just means the folder you’re trying to write into doesn’t exist yet.

claims.text: If 'command not found: ruff' occurs in a venv, install ruff into the virtual environment: python -m pip install --upgrade ruff.
claims.source_excerpt:
(venv) jose@Joses-MacBook-Pro discord-bot % ruff check . > architecture/ruff_output.txt
zsh: command not found: ruff

`ruff` just isn’t installed in your virtual-env yet.

claims.text: Pin dev-tool versions to a requirements-dev.txt to ensure reproducible lint/test runs (example pins: ruff==0.4.1, mypy==1.10.0, pytest==8.2.0).
claims.source_excerpt:
If you haven’t already, create a `requirements-dev.txt` (or add to `pyproject.toml`) and pin versions:

ruff==0.4.1
mypy==1.10.0
pytest==8.2.0

glossary.one_line: LLM responses augmented with retrieved documents or context from a vector store or database.
A neural language model trained on large corpora used for generation, summarization, and reasoning.
A numeric vector representing semantic meaning of text, used for similarity search and retrieval.
Persistent store for embeddings enabling approximate nearest-neighbour search over vectors.
A widely-used library for efficient similarity search over large vector collections (vector store layer).
A driver that composes LLM calls and tool invocations to perform multi-step tasks programmatically.
Mechanism where an agent exposes named functions (tools) to the LLM for external actions or I/O.
A reusable prompt structure with placeholders used to provide context to an LLM consistently.
Providing a small number of examples in the prompt to guide an LLM's desired behavior.
When an LLM produces plausible but incorrect or unverifiable information.
The token budget an LLM can attend to in a single request (limits how much conversation/state can be passed).
A sampling parameter controlling randomness in LLM outputs; higher = more creative, lower = more deterministic.
A local LLM runtime / model manager used to run language models on-prem or locally (non-cloud option).

frameworks.name: ToR → Proposal Prompt Framework
frameworks.definition: A repeatable method for converting a client's Terms of Reference into a high-quality prompt that produces a structured services proposal.
steps: Clarify intent: define the proposal type, audience, tone, and success criteria.
Specify input: indicate exact ToR text or excerpts and any supplementary documents.
Specify output: choose structure (headings), format (Markdown, Word outline, JSON), length and level of detail.
Break down subtasks: analysis, extraction of requirements, draft sections, budget/fees, references.
Provide examples: include a sample ToR excerpt and a sample desired proposal fragment (few-shot).
Set constraints and variables: tone, verbosity, procurement rules, confidentiality notes.
Test and iterate: run completions, evaluate, refine prompt and examples, add rubric or feedback loop.
frameworks.when_to_use: When you must generate a tailored services proposal from a ToR, especially under procurement or client-facing conditions where structure and compliance matter.
failure_modes: Insufficient ToR context causing incorrect scope assumptions
Prompt omits procurement-specific constraints (e.g., public tender rules)
Output tone or level of detail misaligned with client expectations
Budget/fee section not reconciled with stated deliverables

frameworks.name: Prompt Testing & Refinement Framework
frameworks.definition: A concise protocol to validate prompt outputs, detect errors, and improve alignment to client requirements.
steps: Select representative ToR samples including edge cases.
Run the prompt with controlled variables (e.g., fixed temperature for factual outputs).
Evaluate outputs against a checklist: accuracy, relevance, format, compliance, tone.
Flag and document deviations or hallucinations.
Refine prompt: clarify instructions, add examples, tighten format specs.
Repeat until outputs meet success criteria; optionally record a final template and version notes.
frameworks.when_to_use: After drafting an initial prompt template and before using it on actual client submissions or tenders.
failure_modes: Overfitting to the sample ToR and failing on real variations
Missed edge cases from long or multi-part ToRs
Unaddressed hallucinations in experience or references

playbooks.title: Draft a Services Proposal from a Client ToR
playbooks.trigger: You receive a ToR and need a first-draft proposal quickly and consistently.
steps: Ingest the ToR (or paste key excerpts) and highlight mandatory deliverables, deadlines, and evaluation criteria.
Run the ToR → Proposal prompt to generate a structured draft (Introduction, Scope, Methodology, Team, Timeline, Budget, References).
Manually validate that the draft maps every explicit ToR requirement to a proposal deliverable or clarifying assumption.
Adjust methodology, timeline, or fees to align with procurement/contractual constraints.
Create a short change log of assumptions and any client clarifications required.
Finalize the draft and export in the required format (Word/PDF/markdown).
playbooks.applicable_when: Preparing consultancy or engineering services proposals for clients, including public procurement or PPP advisory responses.

playbooks.title: Create a Reusable Proposal Prompt Template
playbooks.trigger: You repeatedly respond to ToRs and want a consistent, versioned prompt template for team use.
steps: Identify variable fields: client name, ToR excerpt, contract type, expected deliverables, constraints.
Draft the base prompt including required outputs and format (headings, length, tone).
Add 1–2 few-shot examples showing desired section-level phrasing and formatting.
Define test cases (typical ToR, long ToR, ambiguous ToR) and run the prompt against each.
Document prompt version, usage notes, and any parameters (e.g., temperature guidance).
Store template in your knowledge system and brief team members on usage and review process.
playbooks.applicable_when: You want consistent proposal drafts across projects or to enable junior staff to generate baseline proposals quickly.

claims.text: OpenAI's Prompt Engineering Guide frames six core prompting strategies: clear instructions; provide reference text; split complex tasks; give examples; specify format; experiment and iterate.
claims.source_excerpt: We’ll use the six strategies outlined in the guide: 1. Write clear instructions. 2. Provide reference text. 3. Split complex tasks into simpler subtasks. 4. Give examples of the desired output. 5. Specify the desired format. 6. Experiment and iterate.

claims.text: For controlled factual output use low temperature; for more creative output use higher temperature (example: 0 for factual, 0.7 for creative).
claims.source_excerpt: Testing prompts with different temperature settings (e.g., 0 for factual, 0.7 for creative)

claims.text: A practical proposal structure for ToR responses includes: Introduction, Objectives/Scope, Methodology, Team, Work Plan/Timeline, Budget/Fee, and Relevant Experience.
claims.source_excerpt: Based on the ToR below, generate a structured draft proposal that includes the following sections: 1. Introduction and Understanding of the Assignment 2. Objectives and Scope of Services 3. Methodology and Approach 4. Team Composition and Roles 5. Work Plan and Timeline 6. Budget and Fee Structure (if applicable) 7. Relevant Experience and References (optional section)

claims.text: When a ToR is long, analyze it in chunks (section-by-section) to avoid missing requirements and to improve prompt performance.
claims.source_excerpt: Use chunked analysis if the ToR is long (e.g., one section at a time)

frameworks.name: Time-vs-Money Targeting Framework
frameworks.definition: A simple financial-first method to set part-time capacity, revenue goals and the required price points to achieve them.
steps: Set a hard ceiling on billable days per month/year (e.g., 8–10 days/month => 96–120 days/year).
Set an annual revenue goal (net/gross as appropriate).
Compute required day-rate: revenue ÷ planned billable days.
Map services to that day-rate (which services justify the price and which don't).
Enforce time-cap clauses, prioritise high-rate, low-effort work and avoid low-margin scope creep.
Monitor utilisation and increase rates if utilisation exceeds target thresholds (e.g., +10% if >70%).
frameworks.when_to_use: When planning to reduce hours but maintain or increase income; useful before rebranding, pricing or client outreach.
failure_modes: Underestimating non-billable time (marketing, admin) and thus underpricing.
Overcommitting to low-rate work that erodes capacity for high-rate offers.
Ignoring pipeline seasonality and ending the year under target.
Failing to enforce time-cap clauses leading to scope creep.

frameworks.name: High-Value Fractional Offer Packaging Framework
frameworks.definition: A packaging approach to convert senior infrastructure expertise into repeatable, premium, low-time offerings (calls, short DDs, retainers, NEDs, productised IP).
steps: Inventory core expertise and recurring productisable outputs (due-diligence memo, board deck, climate-resilience model).
Design a three-tier offering (e.g., expert call, short paid DD, retainer/NED) with clear deliverables and pricing.
Create templated deliverables to minimise delivery time and enable scale.
Define contract terms: payment milestones (100% for calls, 50% on kickoff), time caps, and a master services agreement.
Choose route-to-market channels: expert networks, specialist brokerages, direct outreach to warm clients, board recruiters.
Productise optional semi-passive levers (cohort course, licensing, newsletter) for recurring revenue.
frameworks.when_to_use: When shifting from full-time to fractional/part-time advisory and wanting to preserve margin while scaling limited hours.
failure_modes: Over-engineering productisation before validating market willingness to pay.
Poorly defined deliverables leading to disputes and extra unpaid time.
Relying on a single channel (e.g., only expert networks) and losing diversification.
Underestimating legal/tax implications of retainers or equity-based compensation.

playbooks.title: Transition to a 15–20 Hour Week (Senior Infrastructure Advisor)
playbooks.trigger: Decide to reduce active hours while maintaining or increasing income.
steps: Define billable-day ceiling and target annual revenue; compute required day-rate.
Choose highest-value services you can deliver quickly (expert-network calls, 2-day red-flag DDs, NED seats, masterclasses).
Create a three-tier menu with fixed prices and clear deliverables.
Register on expert-network platforms and specialist brokerages; prepare a condensed CV and rate floor.
Email 20–30 warm contacts announcing fractional availability and attach a one-page offering.
Implement operations: hire a 10 h/mo virtual assistant, prepare templated deliverables, set up invoice and NDA/MSA templates.
Introduce guardrails: no >25% travel, two-month confirmed work runway before onboarding new clients, time-cap clauses.
Track utilisation monthly and raise rates if utilisation exceeds 70%.
playbooks.applicable_when: Best used by senior advisors with recognisable sector expertise and an existing network, ready to productise deliverables.

playbooks.title: Pricing & Contracting for Part-Time Advisors
playbooks.trigger: Preparing client offers or negotiating fees while protecting limited hours.
steps: Set a day-rate from your revenue goals and available billable days.
Offer a simple three-tier pricing menu (expert call, short DD, retainer/NED).
Use a master services agreement (MSA) with standard clauses to speed negotiations.
Require 100% upfront for short calls, 50% on kickoff for projects, monthly invoicing for retainers.
Include explicit time-cap clauses; treat overruns as change orders at a published rate.
Offer quarterly or annual rate reviews (e.g., +10% if utilisation >70%).
playbooks.applicable_when: When quoting project work, joining expert networks, or formalising board/retainer engagements.

playbooks.title: Operational Setup for Low-Intensity Consulting
playbooks.trigger: You plan to limit active work hours and need to protect time while maintaining client service.
steps: Outsource inbox triage, scheduling and invoicing to a virtual assistant (e.g., 10 h/mo).
Create templated deliverables for common outputs (DD memo, board slide deck, course slides).
Maintain a library of standard NDAs and MSAs to avoid repeated legal fees.
Automate lead capture from LinkedIn into a simple CRM via lightweight integrations.
Set strict calendar rules (limited meeting days/hours, no same-day bookings).
Use concise, pre-approved email templates for proposals and follow-ups to save time.
playbooks.applicable_when: Useful immediately upon accepting the first part-time client to prevent admin erosion of time budgets.
